newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION - NZ markets' comfort with Labour a myth.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - NZ markets' comfort with Labour a myth.

text.p: By Roger Kerr, Executive Director, Bancorp.
AUCKLAND, Oct 9 - Three years ago in November 1993, both the financial markets and the political opinion polls got it wrong in picking the outcome of the general election.
Both barometers of opinion expected a comfortable victory for the National Party in 1993 -- the result was a hung Parliament and some turmoil in local financial markets for 2-3 weeks subsequent.

In the leadup to this Saturday's election the financial markets have seemingly been calm and confident that no matter what the election outcome, economic policy direction and the performance of the economy offer no threat to interest rate and currency markets.
The markets were wrong in 1993, have they got it wrong again?

Despite widespread media comment that the market buoyancy reflects a total lack of worry about a left-of-centre government, the reality in the marketplace is that other more powerful influences have to date completely outweighed any
uncertainty/concerns local financial and investment markets may have.

Foreign investment demand for our high yielding interest rates, as New Zealand finds itself at a completely opposite position in the growth/inflation/monetary cycle than other countries (particluarly Europe) has driven down bond interest rates and until this week maintained the New Zealand dollar on its highs.
The timing and volumes of the capital inflows ($5 billion dollars this year to date) from Euro-Kiwi and Samurai issues have very little to do with our election campaign or politicians' promises.

The overseas investors are blinded by the yield return and the weight of money has overwhelmed any local selling of bonds or the New Zealand dollar from people worried about the election and potential changes to economic policy.
Therefore the ability of the local financial markets to reflect a true political risk factor about the future has been distorted by the sheer volume of the capital inflows into Kiwi dollars.
These events have disguised the signals the financial markets would normally provide.
Adding to the complexity of the picture last week was the statement from Standard & Poors that no matter what type of government was elected our sovereign credit rating was safe.

It has not been widely reported that Standard & Poors were forced to qualify their views last Friday, conceding that higher spending fiscal policies that caused budget surpluses to turn into deficits would threaten our credit rating in an adverse way.
We see fiscal policy as the largest risk factor for the markets to assimilate if the election result is a Labour-led left-of-centre coalition.
It is very easy for politicians to spend the surpluses when they are available. Once made, the spending increases are guaranteed, there are no guarantees about future levels of tax revenue.

If the economy underperforms over the next 12 months as the high New Zealand dollar value erodes exporter confidence, investment and production, GDP growth could be well short of optimistic Treasury forecasts and the forecasted surpluses disappear rather quickly.
It appears that the financial markets need reminding that the Labour Party's economic policy plan offers the largest threat to fiscal achievement.
The markets and business leaders seem relaxed at the prospect of Dr Michael Cullen being the next Finance Minister. His commitment to the independent Reserve Bank is reassuring on the surface.

However, some foreign investors may well see the moving out of the inflation target band to three percent as New Zealand going soft on its commitment to low inflation, and accepting a higher limit because the two percent was difficult to achieve
over the last 12 months.

If a Labour-led left-of-centre coalition is the result of the election the markets would be looking for some immediate and concrete reassurances from the new finance minister that spending plans would be postponed if the tax revenue proved to be less than forecast, so as to maintain prudent fiscal control.
Financial market participants will remember the "surplus that wasn't" produced by Labour's David Caygill's budget in 1989. Interest rates reacted to that fiasco and they could do the same again.
As the pundits say "the election result is too close to call", but the markets for whatever reason are giving the impression that they have priced-in a National right-of-centre victory.
The markets' apparent comfort with the Labour victory is something of a myth.

Watch out for some wild fluctuations and volatility immediately after Saturday as the markets have a wake up call on the realities of who may be playing power-broker in the formation of the first MMP elected government.
Any signs of concessions or deals with Winston Peters (NZ First) or Jim Anderton (Alliance) have to be regarded as a threat of fiscal looseness.

Under this scenario the New Zealand dollar would move lower, interest rates staying up as the Reserve Bank are required to keep monetary policy tight to compensate the inflationary impact of a looser fiscal policy.
The New Zealand dollar has already started to fall to reflect late concerns as to what a left-of-centre government might mean for economic policy and economic performance.

Foreign investors have done very nicely in the New Zealand market over recent months, the NZ dollar has appreciated and the bonds increased in value as yields fell under the Euro-Kiwi weight, and following Australian and U.S. bond markets.
It is entirely wise and understandable for U.S. fund managers to be now cashing-up those gains before the unknown of the election.
A left-of-centre outcome could fuel further portfolio disinvestment and push the NZ dollar significantly lower.
(Note - The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters.)
